title: The Event Loop and Async Execution
summary: JavaScript is single-threaded, but the browser isn't — the event loop coordinates a synchronous call stack, Web APIs running elsewhere, and two queues that never run at the same priority. Microtasks always win.

slides.markdown:
"Predict the order these log" is the canonical whiteboard question of frontend interviews, and it's really testing one thing: do you know that JavaScript runs on **one thread**, but the environment around it — the browser or Node — does not.

The call stack executes your code one frame at a time. Anything that takes time — a timer, a network request, a file read — is handed off to the surrounding environment, which finishes it in the background and hands the result back through one of **two separate queues**. Those two queues have a strict, non-negotiable priority order, and that order is the entire trick behind every "predict the output" question in this space.

Get the four pieces — stack, Web APIs, microtask queue, macrotask queue — straight, and every mixed `setTimeout`/`Promise` puzzle becomes mechanical instead of a guess.

slides.subTitle: One frame at a time, synchronously
Web APIs / Node APIs, not the JS engine
slides.markdown:
`setTimeout`, `fetch`, DOM events, file I/O — none of these are implemented **inside** the JavaScript engine. The engine hands them off to the surrounding environment (the browser's C++ APIs, or libuv in Node), which runs the actual timer, network request, or disk read on its own threads, completely outside the single JS call stack.

When that background work finishes, the environment doesn't inject the result directly into your running code — it can't, because the call stack might be busy. Instead, it places a **callback** on one of two queues, to be run only once the call stack is empty. This is the whole reason JavaScript can do "async" despite having only one thread of JS execution: the waiting happens somewhere else entirely.

slides.subTitle: Microtasks vs macrotasks
slides.markdown:
Callbacks waiting to run live in one of two queues:

- **Macrotask queue** — `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, DOM events, `postMessage`. Historically called the "task queue."
- **Microtask queue** — `Promise.then`/`.catch`/`.finally` callbacks, `queueMicrotask`, and `MutationObserver` callbacks.

The event loop's rule, every single cycle: after the current call stack empties, **drain the entire microtask queue — every microtask, including new ones added while draining — before running even one macrotask.** Only once the microtask queue is completely empty does the loop take the next macrotask off the front of that queue, run it, and then drain microtasks again before the next macrotask.

This is why a `Promise.then` callback always logs before a `setTimeout(..., 0)` callback, no matter which was registered first — it isn't about timing, it's about which queue each one belongs to.

slides.sectionTitle: The full loop, end to end
slides.markdown:
One trip through the event loop, in order:

1. Run everything on the call stack until it's empty (all currently-executing synchronous code).
2. Drain the **microtask queue** completely — including microtasks that get added by other microtasks while draining.
3. Take the single oldest task off the **macrotask queue** and run it, pushing it onto the now-empty call stack.
4. Go back to step 2.

Step 2 running to full exhaustion before step 3 ever starts is the detail that trips people up: a microtask that itself queues another microtask delays the next macrotask further, potentially indefinitely.

slides.subTitle: Mixed sync, `setTimeout`, and `Promise.then`
A third timing lane, tied to rendering
slides.markdown:
`requestAnimationFrame` (rAF) doesn't belong to either queue above — it runs on its own schedule, right before the browser's next repaint:

| | Runs when | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **Microtask** (`Promise.then`) | immediately after the current task, before anything else | reacting to async results as fast as possible |
| **Macrotask** (`setTimeout`) | after a minimum delay, after microtasks drain, whenever the loop gets to it | deferred work, polling |
| **`requestAnimationFrame`** | right before the next repaint, synced to the display's refresh rate (~60Hz → ~16.6ms) | visual updates — animations, layout reads |

Because rAF is tied to the paint cycle, it's the correct place to change styles you want animated smoothly — a `setTimeout(fn, 16)` guesses at the frame rate, while rAF is handed the exact right moment by the browser itself, and is automatically paused on background tabs to save battery, which timers are not.

slides.subTitle: An infinite microtask queue blocks rendering
vs the browser's single loop
slides.markdown:
The browser's loop is effectively "stack, then microtasks, then one macrotask." Node's loop, backed by libuv, breaks the macrotask side into ordered **phases**, run in a fixed cycle: `timers` (expired `setTimeout`/`setInterval`) → `pending callbacks` → `poll` (I/O) → `check` (`setImmediate`) → `close callbacks`, then back to `timers`.

The practical consequence: Node still drains the entire microtask queue **between every phase**, not just once per full loop — so a promise chain queued inside an I/O callback in the `poll` phase runs before Node even reaches the `check` phase. This is also why `setImmediate` vs `setTimeout(fn, 0)` ordering is famously inconsistent in Node — which one fires first depends on whether you're inside an I/O callback already, i.e., which phase you're currently in.

slides.sectionTitle: Multiple `.then` calls: still one microtask each
Why `async`/`await` doesn't change any of this

slides.markdown:
A complete answer walks the same four steps every time, regardless of how the snippet is dressed up:

1. **Run every synchronous line first**, in source order, top to bottom.
2. **Sort every deferred call by queue**, not by registration order: promises and `await` continuations go to the microtask queue; `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/events go to the macrotask queue.
3. **Drain microtasks completely** — all of them, including ones added while draining — before touching a single macrotask.
4. **Run exactly one macrotask**, then repeat from step 3.

Said out loud with that structure, a candidate reads as someone who has the actual model, not someone who memorized "promises are faster than setTimeout" — which is a common but incomplete simplification that breaks the moment a question nests a `setTimeout` inside a `.then()` or vice versa.
